paragraphs: I have shown that none of the powers transferred to the federal government is unnecessary or improper. The next question is whether the whole mass of them will endanger the portion of authority left to the individual States.

The opponents of the Convention's plan, instead of first asking how much power the federal government absolutely needs for its purposes, have exhausted themselves on a secondary question: what the proposed degree of power might do to the governments of the particular States. But consider what has been shown. The Union is essential to the security of the American people against foreign danger. It is essential to their security against quarrels and wars among the different States. It is essential to protect them from those violent and oppressive factions which embitter the blessings of liberty, and from those military establishments which must gradually poison liberty at its very fountain. In a word, the Union is essential to the happiness of the American people. Given all this, is it not preposterous to object to a government, one without which the objects of the Union cannot be attained, that it may diminish the importance of the governments of the individual States? Was the American Revolution fought, was the American Confederacy formed, was the precious blood of thousands shed and the hard-earned wealth of millions spent, so that the people of America might enjoy peace, liberty, and safety? Or was it so that the governments of the individual States, those particular municipal establishments, might hold a certain extent of power and be dressed in certain dignities and attributes of sovereignty? We have heard of the impious doctrine of the Old World that the people were made for kings, not kings for the people. Is the same doctrine now to be revived in the New World in another shape, so that the solid happiness of the people is to be sacrificed to the views of political institutions of a different form? It is too early for politicians to count on our having forgotten this: the public good, the real welfare of the great body of the people, is the supreme object to be pursued, and no form of government has any value except as it is fitted to attain that object. If the plan of the Convention were against the public happiness, my voice would be, Reject the plan. If the Union itself were inconsistent with the public happiness, it would be, Abolish the Union. In the same way, wherever the sovereignty of the States cannot be reconciled with the happiness of the people, the voice of every good citizen must be, Let the former be sacrificed to the latter. How far the sacrifice is necessary has been shown. How far what remains unsacrificed will be endangered is the question now before us.

In the course of these papers I have touched on several important considerations that count against the supposition that the federal government's operation will gradually prove fatal to the State governments. The more I turn the subject over, the more fully I am persuaded that the balance is much more likely to be upset by the State scale outweighing the federal one than the reverse.

In every example of ancient and modern confederacies, we have seen the members showing the strongest tendency to strip the general government of its authorities, while the general government was very ineffectual at defending itself against their encroachments. Most of these systems were so unlike the one before us that any inference from their fate to ours is greatly weakened. Still, the States will keep a very large share of active sovereignty under the proposed Constitution, so the inference should not be dismissed entirely. In the Achaean league, the federal head probably had a degree and kind of power that made it much like the government framed by the Convention. The Lycian Confederacy, as far as its principles and form have been handed down, must have resembled it more closely still. Yet history never tells us that either of them degenerated, or tended to degenerate, into a single consolidated government. We know, on the contrary, that one of them was ruined because the federal authority could not prevent the quarrels, and finally the disunion, of the subordinate authorities. These cases deserve our attention all the more because the outside pressures forcing the component parts together were far more numerous and powerful than in our case. Weaker bonds within would therefore have been enough to hold the members to the head and to each other.

The feudal system showed a similar tendency. The local sovereigns lacked the proper sympathy of the people in every instance, and in some instances the general sovereign had it. Even so, it usually happened that the local sovereigns won the rivalry in encroachments. If external dangers had not forced internal harmony and subordination, and especially if the local sovereigns had held the people's affections, the great kingdoms of Europe would today consist of as many independent princes as they once had feudal barons.

The State governments will have the advantage over the federal government by whatever measure we compare them: how directly the one depends on the other; how much personal influence each side will have; what powers each is given; which the people prefer and are likely to support; and how willing and able each is to resist and frustrate the other's measures.

The State governments can be regarded as constituent and essential parts of the federal government, while the federal government is in no way essential to the operation or organization of the State governments. Without the State legislatures, the President of the United States cannot be elected at all. They must have a great share in his appointment in every case, and in most cases will perhaps decide it themselves. The Senate will be elected absolutely and exclusively by the State legislatures. Even the House of Representatives, though drawn directly from the people, will be chosen very much under the influence of the class of men whose hold on the people wins them election to the State legislatures. Each of the principal branches of the federal government will thus owe its existence, more or less, to the favor of the State governments. It must therefore feel a dependence much more likely to breed a disposition that is too obsequious toward them than one that is too overbearing. On the other side, the component parts of the State governments will in no case owe their appointment to the direct action of the federal government, and very little, if at all, to the local influence of its members.

The number of individuals employed under the Constitution of the United States will be much smaller than the number employed under the particular States. There will accordingly be less personal influence on the federal side than on the State side. Think of the members of the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments of thirteen and more States; the justices of the peace; the militia officers; the ministerial officers of justice; and all the county, corporation, and town officers, serving over three million people. They are mingled with the people and personally acquainted with every class and circle. In number and in influence they must exceed, out of all proportion, every kind of officer who will be employed in administering the federal system. Compare the members of the three great departments of the thirteen States, leaving the justices of the peace out of the judiciary, with the members of the corresponding departments of the single government of the Union. Compare the militia officers of three million people with the military and naval officers of any establishment that is within the compass of probability, or, I may add, of possibility. From this view alone, we may pronounce the advantage of the States decisive. If the federal government has collectors of revenue, the State governments will have theirs too. The federal collectors will be mainly on the seacoast and not very numerous; the State collectors will be spread across the country and very numerous. From this view, too, the advantage lies on the same side. It is true that the Confederacy is to have, and may use, the power of collecting internal as well as external taxes throughout the States. But this power will probably be used only for supplemental purposes of revenue. The States will then probably be given the option of supplying their quotas by collections of their own made in advance. And any eventual collection under the Union's immediate authority will generally be made by officers, and under rules, appointed by the individual States. It is indeed extremely probable that in other matters as well, particularly in organizing the judicial power, the officers of the States will be given the corresponding authority of the Union. Suppose, however, that separate collectors of internal revenue are appointed under the federal government. The influence of the whole number could not stand comparison with that of the multitude of State officers on the other side. Within every district to which a federal collector would be assigned, there would be at least thirty or forty officers of different kinds, perhaps more, and many of them would be persons of character and weight whose influence would lie on the side of the State.

The powers the proposed Constitution delegates to the federal government are few and defined. Those that remain with the State governments are numerous and indefinite. The federal powers will be exercised mainly on external objects: war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce, with which last the power of taxation will for the most part be connected. The powers reserved to the individual States will reach all the objects that, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and properties of the people, and the internal order, improvement, and prosperity of the State.

The federal government's operations will be most extensive and important in times of war and danger; those of the State governments, in times of peace and security. Times of the first kind will probably be only a small share of the total, and so the State governments have another advantage here over the federal government. Indeed, the more adequate the federal powers are made for the national defense, the less often will there be those scenes of danger which might help the federal government rise over the governments of the particular States.

Examine the new Constitution accurately and fairly, and you will find that the change it proposes consists much less in adding NEW POWERS to the Union than in strengthening its ORIGINAL POWERS. The regulation of commerce, it is true, is a new power. But few oppose this addition, and no one fears anything from it. The powers concerning war and peace, armies and fleets, treaties and finance, and the other more considerable powers, are all vested in the existing Congress by the Articles of Confederation. The proposed change does not enlarge these powers; it only substitutes a more effective way of administering them. The change concerning taxation may be regarded as the most important. Yet the present Congress has as complete authority to REQUIRE indefinite supplies of money from the States, for the common defense and general welfare, as the future Congress will have to require them from individual citizens. And the citizens will be no more bound than the States themselves have been to pay the quotas assessed on each of them. Suppose the States had complied punctually with the Articles of Confederation, or suppose their compliance could have been enforced by means as peaceable as can be used successfully on single persons. Our past experience gives no support to the opinion that the State governments would then have lost their constitutional powers and gradually been entirely consolidated. To maintain that such a result would have followed would be to say outright that the existence of the State governments is incompatible with any system whatever that accomplishes the essential purposes of the Union.
